The must-sees

  • Bridge of Sighs

    Bridge

    It was built around 1600 to take prisoners from the courts to the new prisons across the canal. The romantic name came later, from 19th-century writers.

    Look for: Look at the small windows barred with stone. Inside, a wall splits the bridge into two passages, so prisoners going in and out never met.

  • Burano

    Neighbourhood

    Burano is known for its needle lace, made here for centuries. Lacemaking is still shown in the island’s Lace Museum.

  • Doge’s Palace

    Palace

    For centuries the doge lived here and the republic’s councils met in its painted halls. Tintoretto’s Paradise in the Great Council Hall is among the largest oil paintings in the world.

    Look for: Look for the lion’s mouths in the walls: stone slots where citizens posted anonymous accusations to the state.

  • Gallerie dell’Accademia

    Museum

    It holds works by Bellini, Giorgione, Titian, Tintoretto and Veronese. Leonardo’s Vitruvian Man drawing belongs to the collection but is rarely shown to protect it from light.

    Look for: Find Giorgione’s Tempest: a soldier, a nursing mother and a lightning bolt, a picture nobody has ever fully explained.

  • Murano

    Neighbourhood

    In 1291 the republic moved the glass furnaces here, partly to protect the city from fire. The Glass Museum traces the craft from Roman times.

    Look for: In the church of Santi Maria e Donato, behind the altar hang large bones said to be from a dragon slain by Saint Donatus.

  • Rialto Bridge

    Bridge · 1591

    Antonio da Ponte finished it in 1591, replacing a series of wooden bridges. For nearly three centuries it was the only way to cross the Grand Canal on foot.

    Look for: On the side of the arch, find the Annunciation in relief: the angel Gabriel on one end and the Virgin Mary on the other.

  • San Giorgio Maggiore

    Church

    Andrea Palladio designed the church in the 1560s for the Benedictine monastery here. Its bell tower has a lift and a view straight back across the basin to the piazza.

    Look for: The façade is two classical temple fronts laid over each other: a tall one for the nave, a wide low one for the aisles.

  • Santa Maria della Salute

    Church · 1687

    Venice vowed to build it after the plague of 1630, and Baldassare Longhena spent much of his life on it. Each November a temporary bridge of boats crosses the canal for the feast of the Salute.

    Look for: Around the dome, giant stone scrolls lean against the drum, which Venetians call the ears.

  • St. Mark’s Basilica

    Church

    It was built to hold the relics of St Mark, smuggled out of Alexandria by Venetian merchants in 828. The bronze horses over the door are copies; the originals, taken from Constantinople in 1204, are inside.

    Look for: At the corner by the Doge’s Palace, four porphyry emperors embrace, looted from Constantinople in 1204. One missing foot was found in Istanbul and is kept there.

  • St. Mark’s Campanile

    Viewpoint · 1912

    The old tower collapsed on its own in 1902, killing no one but the caretaker’s cat. It was rebuilt as it had been and reopened in 1912.

    Look for: At its foot, Sansovino’s small marble Loggetta was pieced back together from fragments found in the rubble of 1902.

  • St. Mark’s Square

    Square

    Every other square in the city is a campo, a field. At high tide the piazza is one of the first places to flood, and raised walkways appear across it.

    Look for: On top of the clock tower, two bronze figures known as the Moors strike the hours on a great bell.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Venice and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Venice passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
